chapter_theme: A song at Pathiripuliyur (திருப்பாதிரிப்புலியூர்): the poet describes the body as a diseased nine-holed hut of flesh and bone, confesses he has no austerity, japa or love, and asks Murugan to come on the peacock and make clear the Upanishads; the praise names Rama's arrow and the vel.

745.reading: The poet describes the body as fat, blood, nerves, flesh, gut, bone and skin packed row on row, an old frame struck by disease and impurities, a hut with nine holes, and confesses that while living in it he has done no austerity and has no awareness, no japa, no restraint, no order, no love; yet before his heart's thought perishes he asks Murugan to come on the emerald peacock with his six faces shining and make clear to him the Upanishad of the four Vedas. The praise names Vishnu who as Rama bent his bow so the ten crowned heads of Lanka's king rolled on the earth, the vel that shook Kailas, crumbled the seven mountains and churned the sea, and Murugan as the teacher at Patalai, where the goddess did penance.
745.nuance: நவதொளை உடைய குரம்பை, the hut with nine holes, is the old image of the body's nine openings. The list of lacks (உணர்விலி, செபமுதல் ஒன்றுதானிலி, அன்புதானிலி) is the poet's self-indictment, and the plea is for teaching, not rescue: நான்மறை உபநிடம் அதனை விளங்க. தேசிக, teacher, names Murugan as guru. அமலை முன் அரிய தவஞ்செய் பாடல வளநகர is the Pathiripuliyur story of the goddess's penance.

links.note: Both see the body as a vessel of filth with nine openings; the Naladiyar uses it to mock the man who praises a woman's arms, 745 to confess the poet's own frame and ask, before thought fails, for teaching.
